Known shortcuts, deliberately left — do NOT fix, they have pending tests:
- non-null assertions: `policy.items.find(...)!` in settleClaim and `policies.get(step.policy ?? -1)!` / `step.incident!` in runScenario. The error tests (unknown item type, damage not in policy, negative amount, more damage entries than insured items) will drive real validation.
- settleClaim mutates policy.remainingCap. That is currently how successive claims share state through the policy registry.

Refactor the implementation while keeping all tests green. Run tests with `pnpm test`. Also verify `npx tsc --noEmit` stays clean.

EXPERIMENT MODE: Run autonomously, return when done.

content.text:
**Rule 1 (Tests Pass)**: 34 passing, tsc clean. Baseline established.

**Naming evaluation (first priority)** — reviewing the claim-side names against what the latest Green phase made them do:

- `settleClaim` — still accurate; it now does the full settlement including cap consumption. Keep.
- `damagePayout` — returns the *uncapped, pre-rounding* payout for one damage. Accurate at its level. Keep.
- `reimbursedAmount` — accurate (amount before deductible). Keep.
- `desiredPayout` — good; names the pre-cap intent that the cap then clamps. Keep.
- **`hasHalvedReimbursement(item)`** — reads as a property of the item, but the domain rule is about the *enchantment level* clause. Acceptable. Keep.

The naming that does *not* fit: the new cap logic inside `settleClaim` mixes three distinct ideas (summing damages, rounding, clamping+mutating the cap) in one function body with no name on the clamping step.

**Rule 2 (Reveals Intent)** — the strongest finding. `settleClaim` has a `reduce` whose callback contains a lookup, a non-null assertion, and an accumulation. The lookup is a separate domain concept ("which insured item does this damage refer to") that deserves a name — and it is precisely the seam the pending "damage not in policy" error test will need.

Let me extract it.

content.text:
Green. **Rule 3 (No Duplication)** — now a conceptual duplication becomes visible that was hidden inside the old reduce callback. Compare:

```
policyBasePremium: [...countByType(items)].map(...).reduce((total, premium) => total + premium, 0)
itemModifierSurcharges: items.map(...).reduce((total, surcharge) => total + surcharge, 0)
insuranceSum: items.reduce((sum, item) => sum + INSURANCE_VALUES[item.type], 0)
netPolicyModifierRate: policyModifierRates(...).reduce((total, rate) => total + rate, 0)
desiredPayout: ...map(...).reduce((total, payout) => total + payout, 0)
```

Five occurrences of the same "add up a list of numbers" knowledge, each spelling out an identical `reduce`. That is textbook Rule 3, and extracting it also serves Rule 2 — `sum(...)` states the intent that `reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0)` only implies.

content.text:
All 34 tests pass, tsc clean, formatting applied.

**Rule 4 (Fewest Elements)** — checked and deliberately declined: `sum` adds one element but removes five duplicated reduce expressions; `damagedItem`/`desiredPayout` add two but each names a distinct domain concept. I also considered inlining `isCursed` and `itemBasePremium`, but they serve Rule 2 and Rule 2 outranks Rule 4.

I left both documented shortcuts untouched as instructed — the non-null assertions in `damagedItem` and `claimStep`, and the `remainingCap` mutation.

## APP mass

Measured on the code I actually changed (the claim path plus the five sum sites):

| | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| `settleClaim` + payout calc | 45 | 20 |
| `desiredPayout` (new) | — | 21 |
| `damagedItem` (new) | — | 9 |
| Four other sum call sites | 44 | 28 |
| `sum` (new) | — | 8 |
| **Total** | **89** | **86** |

Net −3. The extractions add invocations, so the mass win is modest — the real payoff is Rule 3: five copies of `reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0)` collapsed to one. Had I judged only by mass I'd have skipped this, which is exactly the case where Rule 2 and Rule 3 outrank APP.

## One thing worth flagging

`insuranceSum` previously read:

```typescript
items.reduce((sum, item) => sum + INSURANCE_VALUES[item.type], 0)
```

Its accumulator was named `sum`, which shadowed the new top-level `sum` helper. This compiled fine and tests stayed green, so nothing was broken — but it was a live trap: anyone later editing that callback to call `sum(...)` would have hit the accumulator (a `number`) instead of the function, producing a confusing "not callable" error. Rewriting the body to `sum(items.map(...))` removed the shadowing rather than leaving it for a future editor.

## Seam for the pending error tests

`damagedItem` at `/home/experimenter/experiments/runs/2026-09-04_22-18-15_claim-office-example-mapping_v6.1-hybrid-testlist-scope-fix_opus-5-no-thinking/src/claim-office.ts:150` now isolates the policy lookup in one place. Three pending todos ("damage not in policy", "unknown item type in a damage entry", "more damage entries than insured items") all need exactly this lookup to fail loudly — the `!` currently there is the single point where that validation will go, instead of being buried in a reduce callback.

One caveat for whoever picks up the "two sword damages against two insured swords" todo: `damagedItem` uses `find`, so two sword damages against two insured swords both resolve to the *same* first sword. That happens to be correct today (per-damage deductible, and the two swords are identical), but it will not survive that todo or the "more damages than insured items" todo — both will require consuming matched items rather than re-finding them. I did not change it now, since no current test drives it and doing so would be implementing ahead of the tests.

Files changed: `/home/experimenter/experiments/runs/2026-09-04_22-18-15_claim-office-example-mapping_v6.1-hybrid-testlist-scope-fix_opus-5-no-thinking/src/claim-office.ts` (implementation only; no test file changes).
